# Boost Your Learning: Get Quick Explanations and Study Guides with Copilot

**Hook:** By the end of this guide, you'll be able to turn a confusing topic into a clear summary or a ready-to-use study guide in under five minutes — even if you've never used an AI assistant before. This is for students, curious learners, and anyone who wants a friendlier way to tackle tricky subjects.

## Before you start

- **A free Microsoft account** (the same one you'd use for Outlook or OneDrive). If you don't have one, you can create one at Microsoft's sign-up page — it only takes a minute.
- **A device with a browser** (computer, tablet, or phone). You can also use the Copilot mobile app if you prefer.
- **The free plan works fine** for this guide. Some advanced features (longer conversations, image generation) may need a paid Microsoft 365 Copilot subscription, but everything below runs on the free tier.
- **Rough total time:** about 5 minutes for your first summary, and around 10 minutes to build a fuller study guide.

> One honest note: Copilot can explain and summarise, but it can't replace your own reading, lectures, or assessments. Think of it as a study buddy that helps you understand — not a shortcut that does the learning for you.

## Step 1 — Open Copilot in your browser

Go to **copilot.microsoft.com** in any modern browser such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari. You'll land on a clean page with a big text box in the middle and a friendly greeting at the top. Below the box you'll usually see a few suggestion chips like "Travel ideas" or "Healthy recipes" — these are just quick prompts to show you what's possible. **What you see:** a chat-style page with a message input field, a send button (often a paper aeroplane icon), and options to attach images or turn the microphone on. **What happens next:** the page is ready for you to type your first message. **If it looks different:** some people see Copilot inside the Bing search page instead — that's fine, the chat box works the same way. On a phone, you can also download the free "Microsoft Copilot" app from your app store; the layout is similar. **You'll know it worked when** you can see a blinking cursor inside the message box, ready for you to type. 💬 Example: type `Hi Copilot, can you help me understand a tricky topic?` and press Enter — you'll see a short, friendly reply appear in seconds.

## Step 2 — Ask for a plain-language explanation of a topic

Click into the message box and type your topic, then ask Copilot to explain it like you're a beginner. The trick is to name the subject clearly and add the words **"explain simply"** or **"in simple terms"** so the answer comes back friendly rather than textbook-heavy. **What you see:** your message appears in the box, and a short "thinking" animation runs while Copilot drafts a reply. **What happens next:** a few paragraphs of clear explanation appear below, usually with a heading at the top. **If it looks different:** some browsers show Copilot inside a side panel — you can still type into it the same way. If nothing seems to happen, check your internet connection or refresh the page. **You'll know it worked when** you see a written explanation in plain English (no confusing jargon), with key terms spelled out. 💬 Example: `Explain how photosynthesis works in simple terms, like I'm 12 years old.`

## Step 3 — Ask follow-up questions to go deeper

Read the explanation, then ask a follow-up question in the same chat to clear up anything that's still fuzzy. You don't need to start a new conversation — Copilot remembers what you've already asked. This is how you turn a single answer into a mini-lesson. **What you see:** the chat history scrolls up, and a new empty message box sits at the bottom. **What happens next:** Copilot answers your new question while keeping the earlier explanation in mind, so the reply feels connected. **If it looks different:** if the chat forgets what you said earlier (it can happen after a long break), just paste a short summary of the topic back in: "Earlier we were discussing photosynthesis. Now…" **You'll know it worked when** the new answer clearly builds on the previous one, instead of repeating basic facts from scratch. 💬 Example: `Can you give me a real-world example of photosynthesis that I see in everyday life?`

## Step 4 — Turn the explanation into a study guide

Now ask Copilot to package what you've learned into a study guide you can review later. Be specific about the format you want — bullet points, questions, a short quiz — so the result is genuinely useful and not just another wall of text. **What you see:** a longer reply appears, usually with headings like "Key Points" or "Practice Questions". **What happens next:** the study guide is ready to read on screen right away. **If it looks different:** if the format isn't quite right, simply ask again: "Can you redo that as a numbered list?" or "Make it shorter." **You'll know it worked when** you have a tidy, scannable summary with headings, bullet points, or questions you can actually revise from. 💬 Example: `Great, now turn this into a short study guide with 5 key points and 5 practice questions I can test myself with.`

## Step 5 — Copy your study guide somewhere safe

Click and drag to highlight the study guide text, then copy it with **Ctrl + C** on a computer (or **Cmd + C** on a Mac), or long-press the text on a phone and choose "Copy". Paste it into a notes app, a Word document, a Google Doc, or even an email to yourself. This step matters because fresh chats don't carry old answers over. **What you see:** the text becomes highlighted in blue, and after copying you can paste it anywhere you like. **What happens next:** the study guide is saved outside of Copilot, ready for you to read on the bus, print out, or share with a study buddy. **If it looks different:** if copying doesn't work, look for a small "Copy" icon that sometimes appears in the corner of Copilot's replies. **You'll know it worked when** you can open your notes app and see your study guide sitting there, ready to read. 💬 Example: paste it into a note titled `Photosynthesis — quick study guide` so you can find it easily next time.

## Step 6 — (Optional) Ask for a one-line memory hook

Finish by asking for a single sentence or short rhyme you can repeat in your head — these tiny memory hooks (sometimes called mnemonics) make recall much easier during a test or conversation. It's a small step, but learners swear by it. **What you see:** a short, snappy reply appears at the bottom of the chat. **What happens next:** you can write that line on a sticky note, a flashcard, or the top of your study guide. **If it looks different:** if Copilot gives a long answer, reply with "Shorter please — just one sentence." **You'll know it worked when** you have a memorable phrase or sentence you'd feel confident saying out loud. 💬 Example: `Can you give me one short sentence I can remember to recall how photosynthesis works?`

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake:** Asking a vague question like "Tell me about history."
  **Fix:** Add the specific topic, time period, or angle you care about — for example, "Explain the main causes of World War One in simple terms."
- **Mistake:** Treating the first answer as the final word.
  **Fix:** Always ask at least one follow-up question. The second and third answers are usually where the real understanding clicks.
- **Mistake:** Forgetting to save the study guide.
  **Fix:** Copilot's chat is fresh each session on the free plan, so copy anything important into a notes app straight away, before you close the tab.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Next time you read a confusing news article or hear a tricky concept at a dinner party, open Copilot and ask for a plain-English explanation. Five minutes later you'll actually understand what's going on.
- **For your studies or work:** You can build a personalised revision guide for almost any subject — history, science, software, even a new work process — without paying for a tutor.
- **If you're just getting started:** The easiest first move is to pick one topic you've always wondered about, open Copilot, and type: "Explain [topic] in simple terms." That's it — your learning habit starts there.

## Try it now

Open **copilot.microsoft.com** right now, type `Explain how the immune system fights a cold in simple terms`, and read the reply. That's your first study guide — and it took less than a minute.
